# Findings: Rust stable std 1.99.0 `core::net`

No undocumented MUST or grammar deviation was reproduced. The selected slice has documented differences and an unresolved recommendation. No blanket conformance conclusion is made.

## F1: IPv6 link-local prefix and address format — DOCUMENTED

RFC 4291 §2.4 gives the type-prefix entry `Link-Local unicast   1111111010           FE80::/10       2.5.6`. Section 2.5.6 then specifies 54 zero bits after that prefix. The latter yields `fe80::/64` before the interface identifier.

`Ipv6Addr::is_unicast_link_local` explicitly documents the broader prefix. The [source documentation](../published/core-net-src-1.99.0/ip_addr.rs) says exactly: “A unicast address has link-local scope if it has the prefix `fe80::/10`, as per [RFC 4291 section 2.4].” Its examples include addresses outside the stricter format. The result is DOCUMENTED. This is a distinction between a type-prefix predicate and a valid assigned-address format. It is not an unreported grammar violation.

- Reduced input, escaped: `"fe80:0:0:1::"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `666538303a303a303a313a3a`.
- Expected interpretation: Outside the §2.5.6 zero-filled /64 format; inside the §2.4 /10 type prefix.
- Actual: is_unicast_link_local() = true
- Known-item check: PR #85819 removed the strict method; PR #129238 and issue #132506 concern stabilization. These are matching titles in the partial snapshots. Full issue bodies were not supplied.
- Confidence: High for the observed result and documentation. High for the prefix/format distinction.

Reproduction from the target folder, after the offline build:

```sh
sh acceptance/cargo.sh test documented_link_local_prefix_and_loopback
```

## F2: Loopback and link-local scope wording — DOCUMENTED

RFC 4291 §2.5.3 says: “It is treated as having Link-Local scope”. The stable method nevertheless returns false for `::1`.

The [source documentation](../published/core-net-src-1.99.0/ip_addr.rs) says exactly: “this does not mean that the loopback address actually has link-local scope and this method will return `false` on it.” The result is DOCUMENTED. The method is a prefix classifier. Its name alone should not be read as a complete operational scope classifier. Loopback identification itself agrees with the RFC.

- Reduced input, escaped: `"::1"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `3a3a31`.
- Expected interpretation: RFC 4291 §2.5.3 treats loopback as having link-local scope.
- Actual: is_loopback() = true; is_unicast_link_local() = false
- Known-item check: PR #85819 and PR #129238 are related title matches. No supplied title establishes a separate loopback-scope bug.
- Confidence: High for reproduction and the documented exception. Operational scope is outside this value-type audit.

Reproduction from the target folder, after the offline build:

```sh
sh acceptance/cargo.sh test documented_link_local_prefix_and_loopback
```

## F3: IPv4 extraction from special IPv6 values — KNOWN

RFC 4291 §2.5.5.1 says the embedded IPv4 address “must be a globally-unique IPv4 unicast address”. Sections 2.5.2 and 2.5.3 separately define unspecified and loopback values.

The [source documentation](../published/core-net-src-1.99.0/ip_addr.rs) says exactly: “`::a.b.c.d` and `::ffff:a.b.c.d` become `a.b.c.d`. `::1` becomes `0.0.0.1`.” `to_ipv4` uses the bit layouts and also extracts `::`. This is a KNOWN observation with a DOCUMENTED loopback choice. It does not establish that Rust assigns either special value as an IPv4-compatible interface address. `to_ipv4_mapped` returns `None` for both; `to_canonical` keeps both as IPv6.

- Reduced input, escaped: `"::1"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `3a3a31`.
- Expected interpretation: Mapped-only conversion returns None; general to_ipv4 follows its documented extraction rule.
- Actual: to_ipv4() = 1 (0.0.0.1); to_ipv4_mapped() = -; to_canonical() = 6:1
- Additional observation: :: -> to_ipv4() = 0 (0.0.0.0)
- Known-item check: Issue #42174 has the exact title about `to_ipv4` mapping `::1` to `0.0.0.1`. PR #96649 documents this loopback behavior. PR #75019 and #96906 concern the mapped-only method. The snapshots have titles and metadata, not discussion bodies.
- Confidence: High for the conversion results and known-title match. No assignment-policy violation is claimed.

Reproduction from the target folder, after the offline build:

```sh
sh acceptance/cargo.sh test documented_special_to_ipv4
```

## F4: Numeric socket scope syntax and URI syntax — DOCUMENTED

RFC 4007 §11.2 recommends nonnegative decimal zone indices; named strings are optional. RFC 6874 §2 defines `IPv6addrz = IPv6address "%25" ZoneID` for URIs.

The [SocketAddrV6 documentation](../published/core-net-src-1.99.0/socket_addr.rs) says exactly: “_Optionally_, a percent sign (`%`) followed by the scope identifier encoded as a decimal integer”. The quote joins the two doc-comment lines with a space. `%251` therefore means decimal scope 251. URI decoding would treat the `%25` delimiter and remaining `1` differently. `%eth0` is rejected. `Ipv6Addr` alone rejects any zone suffix. This is DOCUMENTED scope, with no URI-parser conformance claim. A missing scope parses as zero, as does `%0`.

- Reduced input, escaped: `"[fe80::1%251]:0"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `5b666538303a3a31253235315d3a30`.
- Expected interpretation: Rust decimal scope is 251. Under URI %25 decoding the zone text would instead be 1.
- Actual: ip() = fe80::1; port() = 0; scope_id() = 251
- Additional observation: [fe80::1%eth0]:0 -> Err(AddrParseError)
- Known-item check: Issue #65976 discusses IPv6 link-local parsing and round-tripping; #82923 requests scope IDs on Ipv6Addr. These titles are related context, not evidence that the present grammar is a defect.
- Confidence: High for numeric interpretation and API scope. RFC 6874 is checked as the supplied historical URI specification, not as a current-standard claim.

Reproduction from the target folder, after the offline build:

```sh
sh acceptance/cargo.sh test documented_socket_scope_is_not_uri_decoding
```

## F5: IPv4-compatible Display and conditional mixed notation — AMBIGUOUS

RFC 5952 §5 states that “mixed notation is RECOMMENDED if the following condition is met”. It conditions this recommendation on recognizing IPv4 embedding from the address field and a well-known prefix. RFC 4291 §2.5.5.1 deprecates compatible addresses.

One reading includes the deprecated compatible prefix and recommends `::8.8.8.8`. Another reading limits the recognizable embedding condition to supported address mechanisms, leaving hexadecimal output appropriate for that deprecated form. Rust prints `::808:808`. Its [textual representation documentation](../published/core-net-src-1.99.0/ip_addr.rs) says exactly: “`Ipv6Addr` provides a [`FromStr`] implementation.” It then references RFC 5952. This explicitly describes parsing; inferring a Display guarantee from that reference would exceed the comment. The observed Display choice does not settle the conditional recommendation for compatible addresses.

Hexadecimal Display for IPv4-compatible addresses is a deliberate, tested upstream choice: coretests `ip_addr.rs:141–143` expects `::c000:280`, the IPv4-compatible case in coretests `socket_addr.rs:34–38` expects `[::c000:280]:8080`, and std `socket_addr/tests.rs:85–89` asserts the same socket output. The supplied [coretests IP source](../upstream-tests-1.99.0/library_coretests_tests_net_ip_addr.rs), [coretests socket source](../upstream-tests-1.99.0/library_coretests_tests_net_socket_addr.rs) and [std socket source](../upstream-tests-1.99.0/library_std_src_net_socket_addr_tests.rs) retain those assertions. AMBIGUOUS refers only to the reading of RFC 5952 §5, not to Rust’s choice or its test coverage. The class is AMBIGUOUS, at recommendation level. No MUST violation is claimed. Mapped addresses use the recommended mixed form. Pure hexadecimal representations of compatible addresses remain legitimate RFC 4291 input and output forms. The formatter oracle uses hexadecimal for these values, so agreement with that oracle does not discharge the unresolved recommendation.

- Reduced input, escaped: `"::8.8.8.8"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `3a3a382e382e382e38`.
- Expected interpretation: Mixed notation if RFC 5952 §5 applies its condition to deprecated compatible addresses; hexadecimal if the condition excludes them.
- Actual: ::808:808
- Known-item check: PR #112606 is titled “Alter `Display` for `Ipv6Addr` for IPv4-compatible addresses”. It is a precise topic match. Its rationale cannot be established from the supplied title alone.
- Confidence: High for observed formatting; moderate for the two readings of the recommendation. An external standards interpretation would be needed to resolve it.

Reproduction from the target folder, after the offline build:

```sh
sh acceptance/cargo.sh test compatible_display_is_hexadecimal
```

## F6: Socket text omits flowinfo — DOCUMENTED

The [SocketAddrV6 comment](../published/core-net-src-1.99.0/socket_addr.rs) says exactly: “It accepts addresses consisting of the following elements, in order:”. It lists brackets, IPv6 text, optional decimal scope ID, and a decimal port. This is an input grammar. The absence of a flowinfo input element is explicit; extending that statement to a Display guarantee would be an inference. RFC 5952 §6 recommends bracketed IPv6 with a port; it does not define serialization of socket traffic-class or flow-label metadata.

`SocketAddrV6::new(Ipv6Addr::LOCALHOST, 0, 1, 1)` formats as `[::1%1]:0`. Parsing that string sets flowinfo to zero. The input grammar is DOCUMENTED. Flowinfo omission from Display is an observation, consistent with that grammar; no explicit Display round-trip promise was found. All address-value round trips pass. All parsed socket-value round trips pass because parsing creates flowinfo zero. No round-trip guarantee is inferred for arbitrary sockets with nonzero flowinfo.

- Reduced input, escaped: `"[::1%1]:0"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `5b3a3a3125315d3a30`.
- Constructed input: `SocketAddrV6::new(Ipv6Addr::LOCALHOST, 0, 1, 1)`.
- Expected interpretation: The documented string grammar contains IP, scope and port; no flowinfo field.
- Actual: The observation test asserts flowinfo=0 after parse(display(x)), while the constructor sets flowinfo=1.
- Known-item check: PR #32429 concerns storage byte order for flowinfo/scope_id, and #65976 concerns scoped parsing. No exact omission-defect title was found. This is a partial-list check.
- Confidence: High for the direct assertion and the documented grammar. No address-text RFC violation is claimed.

Reproduction from the target folder, after the offline build:

```sh
sh acceptance/cargo.sh test documented_flowinfo_not_in_display
```

## F7: RFC 2765 translated prefix — AMBIGUOUS

RFC 5952 §5 states: “mixed notation is RECOMMENDED if the following condition is met”. It requires recognizable IPv4 embedding through a well-known prefix and explicitly names RFC 2765 among its sources.

The input `::ffff:0:192.0.2.1` displays as `::ffff:0:c000:201` on real std 1.99.0. This is an observation, recorded by the real-std proposed assertion. Its six leading segments `[0, 0, 0, 0, 0xffff, 0]` differ from the mapped prefix `[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0xffff]`.

The technical issue is which embedding prefixes a general-purpose formatter recognizes under the conditional recommendation. RFC 5952 §5 names RFC 2765, but the supplied Rust textual-representation comment describes FromStr and does not enumerate Display's recognized embedding prefixes. Treating the historical translated prefix as recognizable supports mixed notation; treating that recognition as outside the formatter's supported policy supports the observed hexadecimal form. This package leaves that policy AMBIGUOUS. Both representations retain the same address bits, and no MUST or input-grammar violation is asserted. The supplied spec directory has no RFC 2765 snapshot, so that RFC's prefix definition and later status were not independently audited here.

- Minimal input, escaped: `"::ffff:0:192.0.2.1"`.
- UTF-8 hex: `3a3a666666663a303a3139322e302e322e31`.
- Expected recommendation: `::ffff:0:192.0.2.1`.
- Actual stable Display: `::ffff:0:c000:201`.
- Known-item check: no supplied title establishes an exact translated-prefix finding. The related compatible-format PR #112606 does not establish a translated-prefix policy.
- Confidence: high for reproduction; the recommendation interpretation remains unresolved.

## Checked with no deviation

The independent model originated in run 1 and was rerun on real std 1.99.0. Current results are in comparisons.txt and counts.json; run-1 receipts are historical. It agrees with the selected grammar and documented socket contract on the recorded corpus. The reference model uses RFC grammar and prefix rules, not copied Rust parser logic. The formatter oracle enumerates zero runs and ranks them by length and first position. Python ipaddress is a secondary comparison only.

`evidence/gen/counts.json` records 195,240 strings, 1,171,440 FromStr calls, 882,222 error returns and 95,723 constructed address round trips. The full port range is checked for both socket families. There are 51 registry blocks and 199 boundary obligations before deduplication. Every first IPv6 16-bit field is checked. Formatting includes every zero layout, widths, fills, alignment and precision. Seed: 42915952. No caught panic or timeout occurred. Python ipaddress accepts 20 zone-suffixed IPv6 strings that the concrete Rust IPv6 parser rejects; that secondary difference is outside the concrete RFC 4291 grammar.

## Limits

The upstream port runs 58 value-type test-file tests and 80 source doc tests (138 total). Excluded DNS, UDP and ToSocketAddrs tests are listed in PORTING.md. The 19 surviving witnesses comprise 12 behavioural cases (7 distinct behaviours; the six whitespace cases are one rule) and 7 optional representation snapshots. Whole-tree search (review, 2026-10-09): the 1.99.0 coretests and benches, library/std net unit tests and TCP/UDP tests, core doc tests outside net, tests/ui, Miri, Clippy and rustfmt tests were searched by content. No covering assertion for any of the 19 named witnesses was found. Std net unit tests and Miri were checked by reading; they were not run under the mutants. This is a bounded absence finding, not a universal proof. One mutant per claimed behaviour does not establish exhaustive coverage. Some mutants invert a predicate; others change a boundary, branch, constant or formatting rule. Most trait, hashing and ordering contracts remain explicit gaps. The independent large corpus has no universal proof weight.

The standalone copy retains unstable helper methods solely for upstream tests. Const trait implementations are shimmed to ordinary traits; stable inherent const tests remain. Other architectures, compiler internals and allocation failure are outside scope. All supplied published sources are hash-checked. Run 1 remains in history. Nightly source differences are recorded in NIGHTLY.md; no second package was built.
